title: Render Performance — Profiling and Common Pitfalls

subChunks.title: Render Performance — Profiling and Common Pitfalls
subChunks.hookHtml: React is fast by default. But developers introduce subtle patterns that undo that performance: creating objects and functions inside render, triggering state updates from effects that create more effects, or reaching for memoisation before profiling. This lesson covers the Profiler tool, the most common performance anti-patterns, and the mental model to reason about React's render behaviour.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Using the React Profiler

React DevTools includes a Profiler tab. To measure:

  1. Open DevTools → Profiler tab
  2. Click the Record button (circle icon)
  3. Perform the interaction you want to measure
  4. Stop recording
  5. Inspect the flame graph — each bar is a component render

The flame graph shows: which components rendered, how long they took, and why they rendered (the 'why' tooltip is invaluable).

Common performance anti-patterns

1. Inline object/array creation in JSX

// ❌ New object every render:
<Component style={{ color: 'red', margin: 8 }} />

// ✅ Stable reference:
const STYLE = { color: 'red', margin: 8 };
<Component style={STYLE} />

2. Inline function creation in JSX (when passed to memoised children)

// ❌ New function every render:
<MemoChild onClick={() => doThing(id)} />

// ✅ Stable with useCallback:
const handleClick = useCallback(() => doThing(id), [id]);
<MemoChild onClick={handleClick} />

3. State updates in effects that trigger more effects

// ❌ Cascading renders:
useEffect(() => { setA(compute(b)); }, [b]);
useEffect(() => { setC(compute(a)); }, [a]);
// b changes → setA → setC → 2 extra renders

// ✅ Derive C from B directly:
const c = compute(compute(b));

4. Keys that change unnecessarily

// ❌ Using array index as key when the list changes order:
{items.map((item, i) => <Item key={i} item={item} />)}

// ✅ Use stable, unique IDs:
{items.map(item => <Item key={item.id} item={item} />)}

5. Lifting state too high

When state that only affects one sub-tree lives at the root, every state change re-renders the entire app. Keep state as low as possible in the tree.

Vex: "Profile before you optimise. Most React apps are fast enough without explicit memoisation. When the app is slow — and you've measured it to be sure — look first at the patterns above. They cause far more slowness than lack of useMemo."

The <Profiler> component for measuring specific trees

import { Profiler } from 'react';

function onRenderCallback(id, phase, actualDuration) {
  console.log(`${id} took ${actualDuration}ms (${phase})`);
}

<Profiler id="QuestList" onRender={onRenderCallback}>
  <QuestList />
</Profiler>

storyBeats.text: A stopwatch, a flame diagram on the wall. Vex points: 'The component that renders in 40ms isn't the problem. The one that renders 200 times per second is.' She circles the tiny component that barely registers. 'Find the frequency, not just the duration.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Performance optimisation without measurement is guessing. The Profiler shows you which components actually rendered and why. Find the real bottleneck — it's almost never where you expect it.

storyBeats.speaker: Anti-pattern: unnecessary inline creation

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Fix five performance anti-patterns in the starter code:

  • Move the inline style object out of JSX to a module-level constant
  • Wrap the item click handler in useCallback so it doesn't recreate on every render
  • Replace the index key with the item's id
  • Remove the useEffect that sets derived state — compute it inline instead
  • Move the itemCount state (which was tracking items.length) to a derived value
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <RealTimeList /> that receives 100 items and updates every second (simulate with setInterval adding a new item). Use the React DevTools Profiler to identify which component renders most. Apply React.memo, useCallback, and useMemo judiciously. Document in comments which optimisations you applied and why.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through the five most common React performance anti-patterns. For each, explain why it causes unnecessary work and what the fix is. Then explain the correct process: why should you profile before optimising?

questions.prompt: What does the React DevTools Profiler's flame graph show?
options: Which components rendered during a recorded interaction, how long each took, and why each re-rendered
The full JavaScript call stack for each render
Network requests triggered by component renders
CSS style recalculations caused by component updates
questions.answer: Which components rendered during a recorded interaction, how long each took, and why each re-rendered
questions.explanation: The flame graph is a visual tree of component renders. Each bar represents a component render with its duration. Hovering shows the 'why' — which prop, state, or context changed. The Profiler tab is the first tool to use for any performance investigation.

questions.prompt: State that only affects one section of the UI lives at the app root. What is the performance impact?
options: Every state change re-renders the entire component tree, not just the section that uses the state
The section renders faster because the state is pre-computed at the root
No impact — React only re-renders components that receive the state as a prop
The impact is negligible — React's reconciler skips unchanged sub-trees
questions.answer: Every state change re-renders the entire component tree, not just the section that uses the state
questions.explanation: A setState at the root triggers a render of the root component and all its children (unless they are memoised). Keeping state co-located — as low in the tree as needed — limits the re-render to only the affected sub-tree.

questions.prompt: Using array index as a key for a list that can be reordered. What bug does this cause?
options: React matches items by key — an index key re-uses the wrong DOM node for the wrong item, causing state and input content to appear in the wrong positions
React throws a warning but the list renders correctly
Items lose their CSS styles when reordered
The list refuses to render because index is a number, not a string
questions.answer: React matches items by key — an index key re-uses the wrong DOM node for the wrong item, causing state and input content to appear in the wrong positions
questions.explanation: When a list is reordered, index keys change meaning: item that was at index 0 is now at index 3. React uses the key to decide which DOM node to reuse. With index keys, it maps the old DOM nodes to the new positions — any controlled input values or local state in list items will appear in the wrong places.
